analysis.headline: Journalists describe a shift from capturing Mexican cartel bosses to killing them, as federal forces hit five FTO-designated cartels in four days
analysis.what_happened: Journalist Jesús Lemus told Infobae that Mexico now seeks to kill top bosses, including the Mayito Flaco and the Chapitos, rather than capture them. Infobae counts members of five US-designated cartels killed or detained in under a week. El Universal reports the Navy deployed more than 1,600 personnel to Sinaloa.
analysis.says_vs_does: The kill-not-capture account rests on unnamed sourcing relayed by journalists, not on a government statement. The record this week shows both: the Navy killed Chuy González Peñuelas in Sinaloa, while Axel Cárdenas was captured alive in Matamoros.
analysis.follow_the_money: Sources do not give a figure.
analysis.at_stake: Lemus frames killings as a way to stop bosses from trading information with US prosecutors, a motive that protects officials named in such testimony. The government gains visible results while US agencies press for action on FTO-designated groups.
tensions: Mexican government vs US prosecutors: a dead boss gives no testimony, while an extradited one can name officials.
Chapitos vs Mayiza: both factions' leaders appear on the reported target list.

analysis.headline: An Ecuadorian judge acquits eight crew members of a boat sunk by US forces, citing no evidence of drug trafficking
analysis.what_happened: A judge in Ecuador acquitted eight sailors from the Don Rufo, a vessel sunk by US military forces in the Pacific, Clarín reports. The judge found no evidence against them and criticised the prosecutor for bringing the case.
analysis.says_vs_does: Washington presents its boat strikes as hits on drug traffickers. In this case the only court to weigh the evidence found none against the surviving crew, who were found days later away from the boat.
analysis.follow_the_money: Sources do not give a figure for any cargo aboard the Don Rufo.
analysis.at_stake: The ruling put the claims behind a US maritime strike before a court. Strike death tolls and cargo claims rest on official statements that are hard to verify independently.
tensions: US military vs Ecuadorian courts: a strike justified as counter-narcotics produced no evidence that held up at trial.

analysis.headline: Primicias maps the network behind Ecuador's eight US extraditions, from Los Choneros to FARC cocaine suppliers and crypto launderers
analysis.what_happened: Primicias reports that eight people extradited to the US link Los Choneros' leadership, FARC cocaine suppliers, cryptocurrency launderers and contacts inside the Ecuadorian state. The US Justice Department called the flow of extraditions historic after Churrón, Daniel Salcedo and Ronald Herrera arrived.
analysis.says_vs_does: The Noboa government presents extraditions as proof of its hard line, and Washington praises it. Primicias reports that 16 investigations and audits target mayors and an ex-viceprefect, mostly opposition figures, so the anti-corruption record falls unevenly across parties.
analysis.follow_the_money: Primicias describes crypto laundering inside the network but sources do not give a figure. Prosecutors cite peculation, gang-linked laundering and illicit enrichment in the local cases without totals.
analysis.at_stake: Extradition moves the strongest evidence about state collusion to US courts and out of Ecuadorian hands. A new curfew in five coastal provinces starts on 1 November.
tensions: Los Choneros vs Los Lobos: four armed structures, including both, are blamed for Machala's killings.
Noboa government vs opposition mayors: most of the 16 corruption files target opposition figures.

analysis.headline: China's embassy in Mexico blames US drug demand and guns for cartel violence while court cases trace cartel money to Chinese brokers
analysis.what_happened: China's embassy rejected US ambassador Ronald Johnson's 28 October remark that an insecure Mexico suits Beijing, El Imparcial reports. It said US drug consumption, arms trafficking and money drive the violence. Guatemalan prosecutors say a laundering network sent most illicit transfers to China and Hong Kong.
analysis.says_vs_does: Beijing's statement lists US demand and guns but omits money laundering by Chinese brokers. A US court has just sentenced Wenshen Xu, a Chinese national in Honduras, for laundering CJNG drug proceeds, and Guatemala traced transfers to China.
analysis.follow_the_money: Xu received a 12-year sentence and a 22 million dollar fine, Infobae and Excélsior report. Prensa Libre does not give a total for the Guatemalan network's transfers to China and Hong Kong.
analysis.at_stake: Each side uses the exchange to deflect pressure over the cartel economy. Johnson's remark and the embassy reply both concern Mexico's choice of trade partners as much as crime.
tensions: US embassy vs Chinese embassy in Mexico: each blames the other's economy for feeding the cartels.

analysis.headline: The US embassy in Guatemala calls a party tied to the Zacapa mayor a narco quinceañera and points to the 2027 elections
analysis.what_happened: The US embassy described a celebration organised by the family of Zacapa mayor Karen Ovalle as a narco quinceañera, Infobae reports. It called for zero tolerance of links between drug trafficking and politics ahead of Guatemala's 2027 elections.
analysis.says_vs_does: The embassy's label is a public accusation, not a charge or a sanction. The cost of the party and its funding have not been explained publicly, according to Infobae.
analysis.follow_the_money: Sources do not give a figure for the party's cost or funding.
analysis.at_stake: Washington gains leverage over candidates through public naming without opening a case. Ovalle's family faces public scrutiny over the party's funding before the vote.
tensions: US embassy vs Zacapa political families: the embassy named the event, while no charges have followed in sources.

analysis.headline: US authorities detain Inés Gómez Mont in Florida after five years as a fugitive in a Mexican false-invoice laundering case
analysis.what_happened: US authorities detained television presenter Inés Gómez Mont, wanted in Mexico for laundering, El País and Ríodoce report. Mexican prosecutors accuse her and her husband, Víctor Álvarez Puga, of laundering money and evading tax by issuing false invoices.
analysis.says_vs_does: Ríodoce notes the detention was not yet officially confirmed when it reported. The record shows she spent five years at large while the Mexican case stood open.
analysis.follow_the_money: The case rests on false invoices used to move money and evade tax, El País reports. Sources here do not give a figure for the sums involved.
analysis.at_stake: Her case puts the false-invoice scheme back before Mexican prosecutors after five years. Separately, Oaxaca police seized 365,865 dollars from three passengers arriving from Dallas.
tensions: Mexican prosecutors vs Álvarez Puga's network: the couple stayed beyond reach for five years.

analysis.headline: Mordisco's dissidents bomb a Cauca toll booth for the second time this month as Colombia's Senate advances the submission law
analysis.what_happened: The army blamed the Carlos Patiño structure of Iván Mordisco's dissidents for a bomb attack on the El Mango toll booth in Cauca, La Silla Vacía reports. It was the second attack there this month, with no injuries. The Senate approved the report for the submission law by 48 votes to five.
analysis.says_vs_does: The submission law offers armed groups a legal exit, yet the Carlos Patiño structure keeps attacking infrastructure. Colombian forces also bombed a Clan del Golfo camp in Nóvita, Chocó, killing six.
analysis.follow_the_money: Sources do not give a figure for the toll booth damage. El Tiempo reports a network stole about a million gallons of fuel to fund the ELN, the Clan del Golfo and Los Pachenca.
analysis.at_stake: Repeat attacks on the same toll booth show the dissidents' reach on Cauca's roads. The law's terms decide what groups gain by submitting versus fighting on.
tensions: Mordisco dissidents vs Colombian state: attacks continue while Congress debates submission terms.
Clan del Golfo vs ELN and FARC dissidents: they compete for routes in southern Chocó.

arc_updates.text: An Ecuadorian judge acquitted eight Don Rufo crew members after a US strike, finding no evidence, as a curfew in five coastal provinces begins on 1 November.
Journalists report a federal shift to killing rather than capturing Mayiza and Chapitos leaders, as the Navy sent more than 1,600 personnel to Sinaloa.
US authorities detained Inés Gómez Mont, wanted in Mexico in a false-invoice laundering case, and Guatemala traced a laundering network's transfers mainly to China and Hong Kong.
Mordisco's Carlos Patiño structure bombed Cauca's El Mango toll booth for the second time this month, and the Senate approved the submission law report 48 to five.
